assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene opened moire quantum matter: flat bands, correlated insulators and superconductivity in a tunable two-dimensional platform. It is a clear case of experiment overturning what theorists expected, and the continuum-model prediction of flat bands at a magic angle has been quantitatively tested. This is the kind of new quantum behaviour in materials that I find most compelling.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald supplied the decisive theory (2011) and Jarillo-Herrero's group the 2018 experimental discovery of correlated states and superconductivity. A fair configuration is theory plus experiment; I propose MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero, though Bistritzer's co-credit for the theory is a real question. Experimental co-discoverers not on the supplied list (e.g. Yuan Cao as first author) cannot be added.
assessment.maturity: Dozens of independent groups have reproduced the phases across twist angles and substrates, and DFT-based and continuum theory agree on the single-particle band structure. The origin of the superconductivity remains debated, but the central discovery is robust and the field is mature enough for recognition.
uncertainties: Mechanism of superconductivity and nature of correlated states are still debated.
Allocation between the theory pair and the experimental group is unresolved, and a three-person limit excludes some contributors.
Sample-to-sample variability (twist-angle disorder) complicates the experimental picture.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Giant tunnel magnetoresistance in crystalline MgO junctions combines first-principles theory of spin-dependent symmetry filtering with experiments that produced several hundred percent room-temperature effects. It underlies read heads and MRAM, and ties computed electronic structure directly to measured transport. Closely related to the 2007 GMR prize but a distinct discovery with a theory-experiment loop I value.
assessment.attribution: Butler and Mathon predicted coherent tunneling and symmetry filtering via Bloch-state decay in Fe/MgO/Fe; Parkin and Yuasa independently demonstrated large TMR in 2004. Three names map naturally onto one theory and two experiment contributions. Credit is fairly clean though the independent near-simultaneous demonstrations deserve scrutiny.
assessment.maturity: Highly mature, widely reproduced and commercially deployed for more than a decade, so recognition is timely if not overdue.
uncertainties: Relationship to the GMR prize may lead some to see it as incremental.
Early amorphous-barrier TMR (Moodera, Miyazaki) is outside the credited set and could complicate priority arguments.
Relative weighting of the two experimental groups is unclear.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum spin Hall effect and the topological insulator concept transformed condensed-matter physics, linking band topology, spin-orbit coupling and protected edge states. The theory is elegant and has been confirmed by transport and spectroscopy, and it connects to first-principles band calculations of real materials.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele introduced the Z2 invariant and the quantum spin Hall proposal in graphene; Molenkamp's group observed it in HgTe quantum wells following the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang (and Zhang's theory credit) are not on this list, which makes the allocation incomplete and contentious. The proposed trio is the best available within the supplied names.
assessment.maturity: Over fifteen years of independent confirmation including ARPES on Bi2Se3-type 3D topological insulators; the interpretation is stable. Recognition is mature and some would say overdue.
uncertainties: The BHZ theory contribution and the 3D topological insulator experiments (Hasan, Kane-Moore-Balents, Fu) are not covered by this candidate.
Kane-Mele graphene gap is too small to observe, so the experimental confirmation rests on a different platform.
Priority with Haldane's 2016 prize may raise overlap concerns.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Aberration-corrected electron optics broke through a limit long thought fundamental and delivered sub-angstrom imaging and atomic-resolution spectroscopy, now routine in materials science. It is an enabling instrument invention of real physical depth and it supplies data that my own theory work is compared against, including EELS spectra.
assessment.attribution: Rose designed the corrector concepts, Haider built and demonstrated the hexapole corrector for the TEM, and Urban led the application to the STEM/TEM in materials. The trio is a natural and widely recognised grouping (Wolf Prize 2011). Others, such as Krivanek on STEM correction, are not in the list and would form a separate claim.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature and ubiquitous; independent implementations are everywhere. Timing is, if anything, late.
uncertainties: Whether the committee views this as chemistry or instrumentation rather than physics.
Competing credit for the STEM corrector (Krivanek, Dellby) is not covered.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamical mean-field theory gave a controlled, nonperturbative framework for strongly correlated electrons, describing the Mott transition and, combined with DFT, enabling quantitative material-specific predictions. It is a major conceptual and computational advance that I know well from the electronic-structure side.
assessment.attribution: Metzner and Vollhardt introduced the infinite-dimension limit, Georges and Kotliar the mapping to an impurity problem and the DMFT formulation, with Kotliar and Savrasov pioneering the DFT+DMFT combination. Metzner, Muller-Hartmann and Kotliar-Savrasov are not wholly captured by the trio, so credit allocation is delicate.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with decades of use and experimental comparison, though quantitative predictive success for real materials varies and nonlocal correlations remain an open limitation.
uncertainties: Prize would be theory-heavy without a single decisive experiment.
Omission of Metzner and ambiguity over DFT+DMFT credit.
Accuracy of DMFT for low-dimensional and strongly nonlocal systems is limited.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold-atom quantum simulation of Hubbard physics gave controllable realisations of models central to correlated-electron theory, including the superfluid-Mott transition, fermionic Mott insulators and quantum gas microscopy. It is a clear example of quantum mechanics offering both new platforms and new insight.
assessment.attribution: Jaksch and Zoller proposed the Bose-Hubbard realisation, Greiner and Bloch observed the Mott transition, Esslinger demonstrated the fermionic Mott insulator. Greiner is credited but I leave him out of the three; the boundary between this and the already-honoured cold-atom BEC prize and other Zoller-related candidates is contested.
assessment.maturity: Mature in techniques, but the headline goal of solving open Hubbard-model questions (d-wave pairing) is not yet delivered, so the maturity of the scientific payoff is partial.
uncertainties: Overlap with other candidates crediting Bloch, Zoller and Cirac.
The simulations have not yet resolved an outstanding condensed-matter question.
Four credited names but only three can be recognised.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, from Katori's magic-wavelength concept to Ye's record-stability implementations, advanced timekeeping by orders of magnitude and enable tests of fundamental physics and relativistic geodesy. The discovery is a clear invention with measurable, reproducible performance.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice scheme; Ye's group realised the leading systems with strontium. The two-person credit is clean, though Hall and Hansch were already honoured in 2005 for related precision spectroscopy and others (e.g. Ludlow, Hinkley) contributed.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed by many laboratories, and a redefinition of the second is being discussed, so recognition is timely. Atomic and metrology physics is outside my core expertise.
uncertainties: I defer to colleagues in atomic physics on priority subtleties.
Overlap with ion-clock work, honoured earlier (Wineland 2012).

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The ATLAS and CMS discovery of the Higgs boson verified the last missing Standard Model particle and is among the most significant experimental results in physics. I treat it as lower on my personal ranking only because particle physics lies outside my field and the 2013 prize recognised the theory.
assessment.attribution: Prize rules limit recognition to three and the collaborations number thousands. Gianotti, Jenni and Della Negra led ATLAS and CMS and Virdee was a CMS originator; any trio omits a close colleague and invites controversy over whether individuals or collaborations should be credited. I propose Gianotti, Jenni and Virdee while acknowledging the choice among the four is unresolved.
assessment.maturity: Extremely well confirmed, with coupling measurements consistent with the Standard Model; timing is mature.
uncertainties: The attribution problem with large collaborations is severe and unresolved.
The 2013 prize partly covered this discovery, reducing urgency.
I defer to particle-physics colleagues on how credit should be allocated.
